name: Copper palmitoyl heptapeptide-14

lead: Copper palmitoyl heptapeptide-14 is a cosmetic peptide complexed with copper and attached to palmitic acid. It is used in anti-aging serums for firmer-looking skin.
It is a lesser-known relative of GHK-Cu, the popular copper peptide.

paras: Suppliers say copper peptides signal skin cells to support collagen and elastin, and the fatty-acid tail helps the molecule enter the skin surface.
Topical cosmetic use; irritation is the usual concern with any skincare product. No human trials of this specific ingredient were found.

studies.title: Activation of latent transforming growth factor beta 1 and inhibition of matrix metalloprotease activity by a thrombospondin-like tripeptide linked to elaidic acid.

chain: Applied in a serum or cream
angle.text: People add it through anti-ageing serums aiming for firmer, smoother-looking skin. The palmitic-acid group is intended to help the peptide sit in the skin's outer layers, and the encapsulation is meant to carry it toward collagen-producing cells.

lead: Copper palmitoyl heptapeptide-14 is a cosmetic ingredient: the copper salt of a heptapeptide joined to palmitic acid. It is added to anti-ageing serums, creams and eye products, where it is marketed for firmer, smoother-looking skin with fewer visible wrinkles. [1]

INCIDecoder lists its official function as skin conditioning and describes it as the payload in an encapsulated copper-peptide technology sold under the trade name X50 Antiaging, in which a polymer-shelled capsule is said to carry the peptide toward collagen-producing fibroblasts. [1] The manufacturer reports, from its own 28-day test in 30 people, an average 33 percent reduction in wrinkles and 19 percent increase in elasticity; that page gives no study design or independent verification. [1]

It belongs to the wider family of copper peptides, the best known being GHK-Cu, which has been studied in small facial trials for firming and anti-wrinkle effects. [2] No independent published human trial of copper palmitoyl heptapeptide-14 itself was found.

paras: It appears in serums and creams aimed at fine lines and loss of firmness, and in eye products. [1] Supplier and manufacturer descriptions attribute collagen- and elastin-supporting activity to it, with claimed activity at about 0.001 percent concentration. [1]

The related tripeptide copper complex GHK-Cu, listed as copper tripeptide-1, is used in anti-ageing and hair products. Wikipedia reports that several controlled facial studies noted anti-ageing, firming and anti-wrinkle activity, but that the trials were small and short. [2]

It is described as the copper salt of the reaction product of palmitic acid and heptapeptide-14. [1] The fatty-acid group makes the peptide more oil-soluble and is intended to help it sit in the skin's outer layers. In the encapsulated version, the peptide sits inside a shell of lactic/glycolic acid copolymer and polyvinyl alcohol, with a second surface peptide said to have affinity for fibroblast receptors. [1]

Once in fibroblasts, the ingredient is reported by its supplier to promote gene expression for collagen and elastin. [1] For GHK-Cu, Wikipedia describes laboratory findings of collagen stimulation in skin fibroblasts and wound-healing effects in animals, mostly from cell and rodent studies. [2]
It is listed in the EU cosmetic ingredient inventory as a skin-conditioning agent. [1] Copper peptides are common in skincare discussions among appearance-focused communities.

No independent studies found for copper palmitoyl heptapeptide-14. The manufacturer reports an in-vivo test in 30 participants over 28 days, without published design details. [1] Studies of the related copper peptide GHK-Cu in skin exist but were small and short. [2]
